# Definition

The __average rate of change__ of $y = f(x)$ with respect to $x$ over the
interval $[x_1, x_2]$ is
$$
\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(x_2) - f(x_1)}{x_2 - x_1}
  = \frac{f(x_1 + h) - f(x_1)}{h}.
$$

## Example 1

A rock falls from the top of a 150-ft cliff. What is its average speed (a)
during the first 2 sec of fall? (b) during the 1-sec interval between second 1
and second 2?

### Solution

Physical experiments show that a solid object dropped from rest to fall freely
near the surface of the earth will fall
$$
y = 16t^2\ \text{ft}
$$
during the first $t$ sec. The average speed of the rock during a given time
interval is the change in distance $\Delta y$, divided by the length of the
time interval, $\Delta t$.

a. The first 2 sec: $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t} = \frac{16(2)^2 - 16(0)^2}{2 -
   0} = 32 \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{sec}}$

b. From second 1 to second 2: $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t} = \frac{16(2)^2 -
   16(1)^2}{2 - 1} = 48 \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{sec}}$

## Example 1: Average speeds over short time intervals

Find the speed of the rock at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$ sec.

### Solution

We can calculate the average speed of the rock over a time interval $[t_0, t_0
+ h]$, having length $\Delta t = h$, as
$$
\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t} = \frac{16(t_0 + h)^2 - 16t_0^2}{h}.
$$
We cannot use this formula to calculate the "instantaneous" speed at $t_0$ by
substituting $h = 0$, because we cannot divide by zero. But we _can_ use it to
calculate average speeds over increasingly short time intervals starting at
$t_0 = 1$ and $t_0 = 2$. When we do so, we see a pattern.

|Length of time interval $h$ | Average speed over interval of length $h$ starting at $t_0 = 1$ | Average speed over interval of length $h$ starting at $t_0 = 2$ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | 48 | 80 |
| 0.1 | 33.6 | 65.6 |
| 0.01 | 32.16 | 64.16 |
| 0.001 | 32.016 | 64.016 |
| 0.0001 | 32.0016 | 64.0016 |

The average speed on intervals starting at $t_0 = 1$ seems to approach a
limiting value of 32 as the length of the interval decreases. This suggests
that the rock is falling at a speed of $32\ \text{ft/sec}$ at $t_0 = 1$ sec.
Similarly, the rock's speed at $t_0 = 2$ sec would appear to be $64\
\text{ft/sec}$.

Geometrically the average rate of change is a secant line.

```{r text_1, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/01-Chapter/01-01-secant.png")
```

## Example 3: The average growth rate of a laboratory population

The figure below shows how a population of fruit flies (_Drosophila_) grew in a
50-day experiment. The number of flies was counted at regular intervals, the
counted values plotted with respect to time, and the points joined by a smooth
curve. Find the average growth rate from day 34 to day 45.

### Solution

There were 150 flies on day 23 and 350 flies on day 45. Thus the number of
flies increased by $340 - 140 = 190$ in $45 - 23 = 22$ days. The average rate
of change of the population from day 23 to day 45 was
$$
\text{Average rate of change:}\quad \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} =
    \frac{340 - 150}{45 - 23} = \frac{190}{22} \approx 8.6\ \text{flies/day}.
$$
This average is the slope of the secant through the points $P$ and $Q$ on the
graph in the figure below.

The average rate of change from day 23 to day 45 calculated in Example 3 does
not tell us how fast the population was changing on day 23 itself. For that we
need to examine time intervals closer to the day in question.

```{r example_3, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}

```
